lessons.title: Drawing Out: Stretching Metal
lessons.body: Drawing out stretches metal to make it longer and thinner. You do this by heating the steel to a bright orange-yellow (around 1,100Â°C) and hammering it on the anvil's face or horn. Start with a 12mm round bar. Heat the first 10cm in your forge until it glows like a setting sun. Place it on the anvil with the hot end hanging over the edge. Strike with the flat face of your hammer, aiming slightly over the edge. Each blow pushes metal outward. Turn the bar 90 degrees after every two or three strikes to keep it square. If you only hit one side, you'll make a flat blade instead of a taper. Work quicklyâyou have about 20 seconds before the metal cools to a dull red. When it stops moving, reheat. For a long taper, like a fire poker, you'll need three or four heats. Use the horn of the anvil for curves and the flat face for straight draws. A 2kg hammer is good for heavy drawing; a 1kg hammer for control. In Africa, many smiths use a simple block anvil made from a piece of railway line. That works fine. Keep your hammer face polishedâdents in the hammer will transfer to the work. After drawing, you can planish with light blows to smooth the surface. Remember: draw out on the anvil's edge, not the center. The edge acts as a fulcrum. If you hear a ringing sound, your metal is too coldâstop or you'll crack it. Quench in water only if you need to cool it fast, but for drawing, let it air-cool or reheat. Practice on scrap rebar until you can make a smooth taper from 12mm to 4mm in three heats.

lessons.title: Upsetting: Thickening the End of a Bar
lessons.body: Upsetting is the opposite of drawing out: you make a bar shorter and thicker. This is useful for making bolt heads, decorative finials, or a mushroom shape on a rod. Heat the end of a 12mm bar to a bright yellow (1,200Â°C). Hold the bar vertically with the hot end down. Strike the cold end with a heavy hammer, or better, slam the hot end onto the anvil face. The force travels up the bar and upsets the hot end. Do this quicklyâthree or four solid hits. You can also place the hot end in a vise and hammer the cold end, but that's slower. For a controlled upset, like a bolt head, heat only the last 2cm. Use a 4kg sledge for the striking blow if you have one. After each blow, the metal thickens and cools. Reheat as needed. If the bar bends, straighten it on the anvil. A common mistake is to hit too lightlyâyou need a solid, direct blow. For a decorative ball on a gate, upset a 5cm section to 20mm diameter, then round it with a hammer. In rural Africa, you can use a large stone as an anvil for upsetting, but a steel anvil gives better rebound. Upsetting requires more force than drawing out, so keep your metal hot. If you see the end turning blue, it's too coldâreheat immediately. After upsetting, you can forge the thickened end into a square, hex, or round shape. Practice by making a 10cm long, 20mm diameter head on a 12mm bar. That's a classic blacksmith exercise.

lessons.title: Bending and Curving Metal
lessons.body: Bending and curving are essential for making hooks, brackets, rings, and decorative scrolls. You can bend cold metal if it's thin (under 6mm) using a vise and hammer, but thicker bars (10mm and up) must be heated to a red-orange (900Â°C). For a sharp 90-degree bend, heat a 5cm section, place it over the anvil's edge, and strike the cold side with a hammer while holding the other end. For a smooth curve, use the anvil's horn. Heat a 10cm section, lay it across the horn, and pull the ends down evenly. For a circle, bend around a pipe or a mandrel. A common method: heat a 30cm bar, clamp one end in a vise, and pull the other end around a 5cm pipe. You can also use a bending forkâa piece of flat bar with two prongs that fits in the hardy hole. For scrolls, bend a series of small curves in opposite directions. Always bend with the grain of the metal if you can. If you bend cold, the metal may crackâwatch for small tears. In Africa, many smiths use a forked tree branch as a bending jig. That works for simple curves. After bending, you can adjust the shape with a hammer on the anvil. For a tight curl, use a pair of scrolling tongs. Remember: metal has a memory. If you bend it too far, it may spring back slightly. Overbend by 5 degrees to compensate. For a decorative S-hook, heat the middle, bend one end 180 degrees, then the other. Practice with 8mm round bar until you can make a perfect 10cm ring.

lessons.title: Twisting Metal for Decorative Effects
lessons.body: Twisting gives a decorative spiral to square or round bars, often used for gates, railings, and fire tools. Heat a 20cm section of 10mm square bar to a uniform orange (1,000Â°C). Clamp one end in a vise. Grip the other end with a twisting wrench or a large adjustable spanner. Turn it clockwise or counterclockwiseâkeep the turns even. For a tight twist, turn 3 full rotations over 10cm. For a loose twist, 1 rotation over 10cm. The metal will shorten as it twists, so allow extra length. If you twist while the metal is too cold, it will crack or shear. Work in one continuous motion. For a double twist, twist one section clockwise, then the next section counterclockwise. This creates a rope-like pattern. You can also twist two bars together: heat both, clamp them side by side in a vise, and twist the free ends together. This is called a cable twist. After twisting, you can flatten the twist slightly with a hammer for a different look. In Africa, twisted bars are popular for window grills and door handles. Use a pipe wrench if you don't have a twisting wrenchâit grips better. For a perfect twist, mark the start and end with a chisel before heating. Twist only the marked section. Quench in oil if you want to keep the twist from untwisting, but usually air-cooling is fine. Practice on 30cm of 8mm square bar: make a 10cm twist with 4 rotations. Then try a reverse twist.

lessons.title: Cutting Metal with a Chisel or Hardy
lessons.body: Cutting hot metal is done with a hot chisel or a hardy. A hardy is a sharpened tool that fits in the anvil's hardy hole. A hot chisel has a wooden handle and a wedge-shaped blade. To cut a 12mm bar, heat it to a bright orange (1,000Â°C). Place it over the hardy with the cut line aligned. Strike the bar with a hammerâthe hardy cuts from below. Turn the bar 180 degrees and strike again. Repeat until the bar is nearly cut through, then break it off. For a cold chisel, you can cut cold metal up to 6mm, but it's hard work. For hot cutting, use a hot chisel struck from above. Place the bar on the anvil face, hold the chisel vertically on the cut line, and hit the chisel with a 2kg hammer. The chisel will sink through the metal. Do not cut all the way throughâleave a thin web, then bend the bar to break it. This prevents damage to the chisel edge. Always wear safety glasses: hot metal chips fly. In Africa, many smiths use a machete or a sharpened leaf spring as a hot chisel. That works if you keep it cool by dipping in water. For a clean cut, cut on the hardy for square bars, and use a chisel for round bars. After cutting, dress the end with a file or hammer. Practice cutting a 20mm bar into three pieces. Remember: never cut cold metal with a hot chiselâit will chip.

lessons.title: Punching and Drifting Holes
lessons.body: Punching makes a hole in hot metal without drilling. You need a punch (a tapered steel rod) and a drift (a larger tapered rod to shape the hole). Heat a 10mm thick flat bar to a bright yellow (1,200Â°C). Place it on the anvil. Hold the punch vertically over the mark and strike it with a 2kg hammer. Drive the punch halfway through, then flip the bar and punch from the other side. This avoids a ragged hole. For a 10mm hole, start with a 6mm punch, then drift it open. A drift is driven through the hole while the metal is hot to enlarge and shape it. For a round hole, use a round drift; for a square hole, use a square drift. After drifting, the metal around the hole thickensâthis is good for strength. If the hole needs to be precise, reheat and drift again. In Africa, many smiths punch holes for hinges, handles, and decorative cutouts. Use a punch made from a car axle or a spring steel rod. Keep the punch cool by dipping it in water every few strikes. If the punch sticks, don't twist itâstrike it out with a hammer. For a clean hole, punch on a block of wood or a lead block if you have one, but the anvil works. After punching, you can file the hole smooth. Practice by punching a 12mm hole in a 5cm wide, 10mm thick bar. Then drift it to 16mm. Remember: punch while the metal is yellow-hot; if it turns red, reheat. Never punch cold metalâyou'll break your punch.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for drawing out metal?
quiz.explanation: Drawing out requires a bright orange-yellow heat around 1,100Â°C for the metal to move easily.

quiz.q: Which part of the anvil is best for drawing out a taper?
quiz.explanation: The edge acts as a fulcrum to stretch the metal when striking over it.

quiz.q: How often should you turn the bar when drawing out to keep it square?
options: B) Every two or three strikes
quiz.explanation: Turning every two or three strikes keeps the bar square and prevents flattening one side.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of upsetting?
options: B) To make metal shorter and thicker
quiz.explanation: Upsetting thickens the end of a bar by making it shorter.

quiz.q: What is the correct technique for upsetting a bar?
options: B) Hammer the cold end while the hot end is down
quiz.explanation: Striking the cold end drives force into the hot end, thickening it.

quiz.q: What color indicates the metal is too cold for upsetting?
quiz.explanation: Blue means the metal is too cold and will crack if struck.

quiz.q: What tool can be used as a bending jig in rural Africa?
quiz.explanation: A forked tree branch can serve as a simple bending fork.

quiz.q: When bending thick metal, what temperature is needed?
quiz.explanation: Thick bars must be heated to red-orange for bending.

quiz.q: How much should you overbend to compensate for springback?
quiz.explanation: Overbending by about 5 degrees compensates for the metal's springback.

quiz.q: What is a common decorative effect made by twisting?
quiz.explanation: Twisting creates a spiral pattern on the bar.

quiz.q: How many rotations make a tight twist over 10cm?
quiz.explanation: Three full rotations over 10cm gives a tight twist.

quiz.q: What happens to the length of a bar when twisted?
quiz.explanation: Twisting shortens the bar, so allow extra length.

quiz.q: What is a cable twist?
quiz.explanation: A cable twist involves twisting two bars together.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for cutting hot metal from below?
quiz.explanation: A hardy fits in the anvil's hardy hole and cuts from below.

quiz.q: What should you do when cutting with a chisel to avoid damaging the edge?
options: A) Cut all the way through
B) Leave a thin web and break it
quiz.explanation: Leaving a thin web and breaking the bar prevents chisel damage.

quiz.q: Why should you wear safety glasses when cutting?
options: B) To protect from flying chips
quiz.explanation: Hot metal chips can fly and injure your eyes.

quiz.q: What can be used as a hot chisel in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A machete or sharpened leaf spring can serve as a hot chisel.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a drift?
options: B) To enlarge and shape a hole
quiz.explanation: A drift is driven through a punched hole to enlarge and shape it.

quiz.q: What temperature is needed for punching?
quiz.explanation: Punching requires a bright yellow heat for the metal to flow.

quiz.q: Why should you punch from both sides?
options: A) To make a bigger hole
B) To avoid a ragged hole
quiz.explanation: Punching from both sides prevents a ragged exit hole.

quiz.q: What happens to the metal around a punched hole?
quiz.explanation: The metal around the hole thickens, adding strength.

quiz.q: What should you do if your punch sticks in the hole?
options: B) Strike it out with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Striking the punch out with a hammer is safer than twisting.

quiz.q: What is a good material for making a punch?
options: B) Car axle or spring steel
quiz.explanation: Car axle or spring steel is tough and suitable for punches.

quiz.q: How often should you cool a punch in water?
quiz.explanation: Cooling every few strikes prevents the punch from overheating.

quiz.q: What is the first step in drawing out a taper?
quiz.explanation: Heat only the section you want to draw out, starting with the first 10cm.

quiz.q: What hammer weight is good for heavy drawing?
quiz.explanation: A 2kg hammer provides enough force for heavy drawing.

quiz.q: What sound indicates the metal is too cold?
quiz.explanation: A ringing sound means the metal is too cold and may crack.

quiz.q: What is a common use for upsetting in blacksmithing?
quiz.explanation: Upsetting is used to form bolt heads and similar thickened ends.

quiz.q: What is the best way to bend a tight circle?
options: B) Use a pipe or mandrel
quiz.explanation: Bending around a pipe or mandrel creates a smooth circle.

quiz.q: What should you do before twisting to ensure even twists?
options: A) Mark start and end with a chisel
quiz.explanation: Marking the section with a chisel helps keep the twist even.
